stem: Students investigate the unique properties of water and how those properties support life.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-025

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that breaking hydrogen bonds between water molecules requires energy input.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Breaking hydrogen bonds between water molecules requires energy input.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Breaking hydrogen bonds between water molecules requires energy input.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that water absorbs a large amount of heat before its temperature rises, stabilizing temperatures.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Water absorbs a large amount of heat before its temperature rises, stabilizing temperatures.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Water absorbs a large amount of heat before its temperature rises, stabilizing temperatures.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that polar water molecules surround and separate ions in solution.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Polar water molecules surround and separate ions in solution.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Polar water molecules surround and separate ions in solution.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the positive (hydrogen) ends of water attract Cl-, and the negative (oxygen) ends attract Na+.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: The positive (hydrogen) ends of water attract Cl-, and the negative (oxygen) ends attract Na+.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The positive (hydrogen) ends of water attract Cl-, and the negative (oxygen) ends attract Na+.

canonical_answer_1:
Hydrogen bonds between water molecules create cohesion, adhesion, and high specific heat, all critical for living systems.

Heat must be supplied to disrupt the transient hydrogen-bond network among water molecules before their molecular motion can increase substantially.

Because incoming energy is spent disrupting hydrogen bonds, a given heat input produces only a small temperature increase. This high specific heat buffers organisms and aquatic habitats against rapid temperature swings.

Water's polarity makes it an excellent solvent for ionic and polar molecules, facilitating biochemical reactions.

Water forms hydration shells around dissolved salt ions. Its polar molecules orient at each ion and keep oppositely charged ions separated in solution.

The partially positive hydrogens point toward Cl⁻, whereas the partially negative oxygen points toward Na⁺. These ion-dipole attractions stabilize both ions in water.
canonical_answer_2: Water's polarity makes it an excellent solvent for ionic and polar molecules, facilitating biochemical reactions.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains the function of one of the identified structures (e.g., the nucleus houses DNA for gene regulation).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Explains the function of one of the identified structures (e.g., the nucleus houses DNA for gene regulation).

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that lacking membrane-bound organelles reduces the energy and material cost of building the cell.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Lacking membrane-bound organelles reduces the energy and material cost of building the cell.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Lacking membrane-bound organelles reduces the energy and material cost of building the cell.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: The simpler cell structure allows prokaryotes to replicate faster.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The simpler cell structure allows prokaryotes to replicate faster.

canonical_answer_1:
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus; their DNA is in the nucleoid region.

The plant cell shows a membrane-bound nucleus and mitochondria, structures a bacterium lacks; a photosynthetic plant cell may also contain chloroplasts.

The nucleus encloses the chromosomes and separates transcription from cytoplasmic translation, allowing regulated access to DNA and its gene products.

Eukaryotes have compartmentalized organelles that allow specialization of metabolic functions.

A bacterium does not spend resources constructing and maintaining internal membrane-bound compartments, so less membrane, protein, and energy are required to build each cell.

With a small genome and no organelle-assembly requirement, a prokaryotic cell can copy its DNA and divide by binary fission rapidly when resources are abundant.
canonical_answer_2: Eukaryotes have compartmentalized organelles that allow specialization of metabolic functions.

The membrane that originally bounded the aerobic bacterium was retained inside the engulfment membrane and became the mitochondrial inner membrane, where bacterial-like respiratory machinery remains.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain, in terms of fatty acid tail structure, why Bilayer B is more fluid than Bilayer A at the same temperature.

(b) Explain how the presence of cholesterol affects membrane fluidity in each bilayer at 20°C versus 40°C.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-031
stimulus: A researcher compares the fluidity of two synthetic phospholipid bilayers at 20°C: Bilayer A is composed of phospholipids with saturated fatty acid tails, and Bilayer B is composed of phospholipids with unsaturated fatty acid tails. Bilayer B is measured to be substantially more fluid than Bilayer A at the same temperature. The researcher then re-tests both bilayers with cholesterol embedded in the membrane, comparing fluidity at 20°C and at 40°C.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The double bond bends the hydrocarbon tail, preventing phospholipids from packing tightly, which increases membrane fluidity.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why unsaturated fatty acids increase membrane fluidity.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the double bond creates a kink in the tail, preventing tight packing of phospholipids, so the membrane remains fluid.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Cholesterol reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents solidification at low temperatures, acting as a fluidity buffer.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain the role of cholesterol in maintaining membrane fluidity across a range of temperatures.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States cholesterol stabilizes fluidity: restricts movement at high temp (prevents too fluid) and prevents packing at low temp (prevents solidifying).

canonical_answer_1:
Unsaturated fatty acid tails have kinks from double bonds, preventing tight packing and keeping the membrane fluid at lower temperatures.

Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer: at high temperatures it restricts movement; at low temperatures it prevents crystallization.
canonical_answer_2: Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer: at high temperatures it restricts movement; at low temperatures it prevents crystallization.

stem: Cells take up glucose via facilitated diffusion using glucose transporter (GLUT) proteins, even though glucose is a large polar molecule.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-032

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that glucose is a large, polar molecule.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Glucose is a large, polar molecule.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Glucose is a large, polar molecule.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer repels polar molecules like glucose.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: The hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer repels polar molecules like glucose.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer repels polar molecules like glucose.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that facilitated diffusion moves molecules down their concentration gradient without using ATP.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Facilitated diffusion moves molecules down their concentration gradient without using ATP.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Facilitated diffusion moves molecules down their concentration gradient without using ATP.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that active transport moves molecules against their concentration gradient and requires ATP.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Active transport moves molecules against their concentration gradient and requires ATP.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Active transport moves molecules against their concentration gradient and requires ATP.

canonical_answer_1:
GLUT proteins are transmembrane channel proteins that allow glucose to move down its concentration gradient without ATP.

Glucose contains several hydroxyl groups, making it strongly polar, and its six-carbon ring is too large to pass easily between phospholipids.

The bilayer core consists of nonpolar fatty-acid tails, so moving polar glucose through that region is energetically unfavorable. A GLUT protein supplies a hydrophilic route across the membrane.

Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it uses a protein carrier and is saturable (limited by transporter number).

If transport carries a solute from lower to higher concentration, the movement is uphill and cannot be powered by diffusion. Active transport couples that movement to ATP hydrolysis or another stored-energy gradient.
canonical_answer_2: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it uses a protein carrier and is saturable (limited by transporter number).

frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The membrane invaginates and a vesicle pinches off, carrying the ligand into the cytoplasm.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Only molecules that match the shape of a specific cell-surface receptor bind and are taken up.

canonical_answer_1:
The virus binds specific surface receptors; the membrane invaginates to form a clathrin-coated pit, then pinches off as an endosome.

Inside the endosome, low pH causes viral envelope fusion with the membrane, releasing viral contents into the cytoplasm.

Influenza enters only after its surface ligand fits and binds the corresponding host-cell receptor. Molecules lacking that molecular fit are not concentrated into the receptor-mediated endocytic vesicle.

Receptor-ligand recognition selects the cargo before membrane invagination, so the cell internalizes bound targets rather than taking up extracellular material indiscriminately.
canonical_answer_2: Inside the endosome, low pH causes viral envelope fusion with the membrane, releasing viral contents into the cytoplasm.

stem: A student compares ATP production in aerobic respiration versus fermentation in yeast under different oxygen conditions.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-036

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the ETC/chemiosmosis generates approximately 30 ATP.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States aerobic respiration uses the ETC/chemiosmosis to generate approximately 30 ATP from NADH/FADH2.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis produce the majority of ATP aerobically.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that fermentation nets only 2 ATP, from glycolysis.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States fermentation produces only 2 ATP via glycolysis.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States glycolysis alone (without the ETC) yields 2 ATP.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that fermentation regenerates NAD+ via pyruvate reduction.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States fermentation regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States pyruvate acts as the electron acceptor that regenerates NAD+.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that regenerated NAD+ lets glycolysis keep running.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains this allows glycolysis to continue producing 2 ATP per glucose.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Connects regenerated NAD+ to glycolysis continuing to run.

canonical_answer_1:
Aerobic respiration yields ~30-32 ATP per glucose via glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.

With oxygen available as the terminal electron acceptor, NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the respiratory chain. Proton pumping and ATP synthase then supply most of the roughly 30 ATP obtained per glucose.

Fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue but yields only 2 ATP per glucose.
canonical_answer_2: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue but yields only 2 ATP per glucose.

stem: A toxin blocks ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane of liver cells.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-038

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that protons flow through ATP synthase down their gradient.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States protons flow down their gradient through ATP synthase.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States proton flow through ATP synthase from high to low concentration.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the released energy converts ADP to ATP.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States the energy released phosphorylates ADP to ATP.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the proton-motive-force energy is used to phosphorylate ADP.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that ATP levels drop sharply because chemiosmosis stops.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predicts ATP levels drop dramatically because oxidative phosphorylation stops.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that blocking ATP synthase halts chemiosmotic ATP production.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that only substrate-level phosphorylation (2-4 ATP) remains available.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains only substrate-level phosphorylation (2-4 ATP total per glucose) remains.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States glycolysis and the Krebs cycle's substrate-level phosphorylation still contribute a small amount of ATP.

canonical_answer_1:
ATP synthase uses the proton gradient built by the ETC to synthesize ATP via chemiosmosis.

Normally, the electron-transport chain builds a high H⁺ concentration in the intermembrane space, and H⁺ returns to the matrix through ATP synthase down its electrochemical gradient.

Proton movement rotates or changes the conformation of ATP synthase, coupling the proton-motive force to phosphorylation of ADP with inorganic phosphate to form ATP.

Blocking ATP synthase causes the proton gradient to build up and prevents oxidative phosphorylation without stopping electron flow.

Blocking ATP synthase eliminates oxidative phosphorylation. The cell can still make only the small substrate-level yield from glycolysis and the citric-acid cycle—about 2–4 ATP per glucose, depending on which pathways continue.
canonical_answer_2: Blocking ATP synthase causes the proton gradient to build up and prevents oxidative phosphorylation without stopping electron flow.

frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: The dimerized RTKs autophosphorylate tyrosine residues, creating docking sites for relay proteins.

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: A permanently active RTK sends continuous growth signals even without growth factor present.

canonical_answer_1:
RTK dimerizes upon ligand binding; each receptor phosphorylates tyrosine residues on the other (autophosphorylation).

Phosphorylated RTK recruits intracellular relay proteins that activate transcription factors, promoting cell division.

A constitutively active RTK phosphorylates itself and downstream relay proteins without ligand binding, so the cell receives a growth-factor signal continuously.

stem: In peas, yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y) and round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r). Two dihybrid plants (YyRr x YyRr) are crossed.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-045

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Independent assortment of the two genes produces a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict the phenotypic ratio of offspring from the YyRr x YyRr cross and explain why.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States 9 yellow round : 3 yellow wrinkled : 3 green round : 1 green wrinkled; explains independent assortment.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The probability of YYRR is (1/4)(1/4) = 1/16, applying the product rule for independent events.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Calculate the probability of producing a plant that is homozygous dominant for both traits.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16; must show multiplication of individual probabilities.

canonical_answer_1:
Independent assortment produces four phenotypic classes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio when genes are on different chromosomes.

Each gene segregates independently; the probability of each phenotypic combination is the product of individual gene probabilities.

For Yy × Yy, P(YY) = 1/4; independently, Rr × Rr gives P(RR) = 1/4. The product rule gives P(YYRR) = (1/4)(1/4) = 1/16.
canonical_answer_2: Each gene segregates independently; the probability of each phenotypic combination is the product of individual gene probabilities.

stem: Red-green color blindness is an X-linked recessive trait. A carrier woman (X^B X^b) has children with a man who has normal vision (X^B Y).
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-046

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that sons get their only X chromosome from their carrier mother.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States sons inherit their X chromosome from their mother, and the mother is a carrier (50% X^b).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the X-linked inheritance pattern from a carrier mother to sons.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State the final probability that a son is color blind, 1/2.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Concludes 1/2 of sons will be color blind.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the final probability, 1/2.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that daughters always receive X^B from their father.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States daughters receive X^B from their father.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the father contributes a normal X^B allele to all daughters.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that daughters cannot be color blind since they cannot be X^b X^b.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Concludes daughters can be at most carriers, never homozygous recessive.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States daughters cannot be X^b X^b given the father's contribution.

canonical_answer_1:
Sons receive the Y chromosome from their father and one X from their mother; daughters receive one X from each parent.

A carrier mother passes the recessive allele to half her sons (who are affected) and half her daughters (who are carriers).

Every daughter receives the father's normal Xᴮ chromosome. Even if she inherits Xᵇ from the carrier mother, her genotype is XᴮXᵇ, so she can be a carrier but cannot be XᵇXᵇ and color-blind in this cross.
canonical_answer_2: A carrier mother passes the recessive allele to half her sons (who are affected) and half her daughters (who are carriers).

canonical_answer_1:
Nondisjunction at meiosis I produces gametes with two copies of a chromosome or no copies, leading to aneuploidy.

During meiosis I nondisjunction, the homologous pair attaches or moves to the same pole instead of separating to opposite poles. One daughter cell therefore receives both homologs and the other receives neither.

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) results from a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21 fertilizing a normal gamete.

canonical_answer_1:
Sea otters are a keystone species: their removal causes a trophic cascade that fundamentally changes the ecosystem.

Sea otters qualify as a keystone species because their effect on community structure is much larger than their abundance alone would predict.

Hunting removes predation pressure on sea urchins, the urchin population expands, and intensified grazing strips away kelp. Loss of the kelp forest then alters the wider reef community.

Removing a keystone predator allows its prey population to explode, which overgrazes producers and collapses the community.

canonical_answer_1:
Predator-prey cycles are driven by time-delayed feedback: prey increase causes predator increase, which reduces prey.

More wolves increase predation and drive moose numbers down. Scarcer prey then lowers wolf survival and reproduction; as wolves decline, predation relaxes, moose recover, and the delayed cycle begins again.

Classic Lotka-Volterra dynamics predict oscillating cycles where predator peaks follow prey peaks by a time lag. If all wolves were removed, the main top-down check on the moose population would be eliminated. Moose numbers would likely increase rapidly (predator release) until limited instead by bottom-up factors such as food availability (overgrazing) and density-dependent effects like starvation and disease, rather than by predation.

canonical_answer_1:
Water potential (psi) = osmotic potential + pressure potential; water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) psi.

Net water movement is from the soil solution into the plant cell because the cell begins with the lower water potential.

Osmosis carries water across the selectively permeable membrane from the soil's higher, less negative water potential toward the cell's lower, more negative value.

Solutes lower osmotic potential, making psi more negative and drawing water in; turgor pressure raises pressure potential.

Incoming water expands the vacuole and pushes the plasma membrane against the cell wall, increasing pressure potential and turgor.

Rising pressure potential makes the cell's total water potential less negative, shrinking the soil-to-cell gradient. Net entry slows until the two water potentials are equal.

stem: During meiosis, a cell with four chromosomes (2n=4) undergoes both meiosis I and meiosis II.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: After meiosis I, 2 cells each contain 2 chromosomes (2 chromatids each); after meiosis II, 4 cells each contain 1 single chromatid.

frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment (metaphase I) generate new allele combinations.

canonical_answer_1:
Meiosis I separates homologous pairs (reducing ploidy from 2n to n); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

Because 2n = 4, the haploid number is n = 2. Homologs separate in meiosis I, producing two cells that each have two chromosomes, with two sister chromatids per chromosome. Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, producing four cells that each retain two chromosomes, now with one chromatid per chromosome.

Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment together generate genetic diversity in gametes.
canonical_answer_2: Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment together generate genetic diversity in gametes.

canonical_answer_1:
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences; gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size.

A restriction enzyme binds its particular palindromic recognition sequence and cleaves the phosphodiester backbones there. Consequently, the distances between successive recognition sites determine the lengths of the DNA fragments.

Smaller DNA fragments migrate faster through the gel; a DNA ladder is used to estimate fragment sizes.

Negatively charged DNA is pulled through the gel toward the positive electrode. Short fragments pass through gel pores more readily and travel farther than long fragments; matching each band to a DNA ladder estimates its size.

Secondary succession begins after a disturbance where soil and some organisms remain, proceeding faster than primary succession.

After the fire, mineral-rich soil, microbes, roots, and buried seeds remain, so plants can reestablish immediately. Primary succession starts on bare substrate and must first generate soil, making it slower.

Pioneer species such as grasses and shrubs re-colonize the burned area first; eventually shade-tolerant climax species return.

Sun-loving pioneers dominate the open site first, but their canopy creates shade that inhibits their own seedlings. Shade-tolerant trees can recruit beneath that canopy and eventually replace the pioneers in the mature community.
canonical_answer_2: Pioneer species such as grasses and shrubs re-colonize the burned area first; eventually shade-tolerant climax species return.

stem: A researcher studying protein structure finds that a single amino acid substitution causes a protein to misfold and lose function.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-080

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the new R group disrupts the interactions maintaining shape.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States the R-group change alters the interactions maintaining the protein's 3D shape.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that a different R group changes the chemical interactions holding tertiary structure together.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that an altered active site or binding surface causes loss of function.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains this can alter the active site or binding surface, causing loss of function.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Connects disrupted shape to a changed active site/binding surface.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that primary structure is directly changed by the mutation.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States primary structure is the level directly changed by the mutation (the amino acid sequence itself).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that primary structure -- the sequence -- is what a single amino-acid substitution directly alters.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the resulting loss of function comes from disrupted tertiary-structure folding.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States tertiary structure is the level whose altered folding, caused by the primary-sequence change, is responsible for the loss of function.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that tertiary structure's disrupted folding, downstream of the primary-sequence change, causes the functional loss.

canonical_answer_1:
Protein shape depends on interactions among R groups: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and disulfide bridges.

A substituted side chain can change ionic, hydrogen-bond, hydrophobic, or disulfide interactions during folding. If the resulting shape changes an active site or binding interface, the protein no longer binds its partner correctly and loses function.

Changing one amino acid can disrupt these interactions and alter secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure.

The mutation directly alters primary structure because primary structure is the linear amino-acid sequence, and one residue in that sequence has been replaced.

Changed side-chain interactions can redirect folding of the polypeptide, altering its three-dimensional tertiary structure. That downstream shape change, rather than the sequence label itself, disrupts the functional site.
canonical_answer_2: Changing one amino acid can disrupt these interactions and alter secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure.

title: APBIO-FRQ-S-081

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State somatic cells are body cells that are not passed on to offspring
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States somatic cells are body cells that are not passed on to offspring
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States somatic cells are body cells that are not passed on to offspring

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States only mutations in gametes (egg or sperm) are heritable
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States only mutations in gametes (egg or sperm) are heritable

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State a proto-oncogene mutation causes overactive/uncontrolled growth signaling (stuck "gas pedal")
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States a proto-oncogene mutation causes overactive/uncontrolled growth signaling (stuck "gas pedal")
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States a proto-oncogene mutation causes overactive/uncontrolled growth signaling (stuck "gas pedal")

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State a tumor suppressor mutation removes the ability to halt division (lost "brake"), and both mutations together are needed to bypass cell cycle controls
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States a tumor suppressor mutation removes the ability to halt division (lost "brake"), and both mutations together are needed to bypass cell cycle controls
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States a tumor suppressor mutation removes the ability to halt division (lost "brake"), and both mutations together are needed to bypass cell cycle controls

canonical_answer_1:
Somatic mutations affect only the individual; germline mutations in gametes can be inherited.

Cancer arises from somatic mutations accumulating in genes that control cell division (proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressors).

An activating proto-oncogene mutation can keep a growth-signaling protein on without an external signal, continually pushing the skin cell toward another division.

Loss of a tumor-suppressor removes a checkpoint that would stop division or trigger repair or apoptosis. Combined with constitutive growth signaling, the missing brake lets the mutant somatic lineage proliferate uncontrollably.
canonical_answer_2: Cancer arises from somatic mutations accumulating in genes that control cell division (proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressors).

stem: A tropical plant has adapted to very low phosphorus soils by forming associations with mycorrhizal fungi.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-084

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that fungal hyphae extend into soil beyond the root system.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States fungal hyphae extend beyond the root's reach into soil.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States hyphae reach further into soil than roots alone.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that the extended hyphal network increases phosphorus-absorbing surface area.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains this increases the surface area for phosphorus absorption.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Connects extended hyphal reach to increased absorptive surface area.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the plant receives phosphorus (and water) from the fungus.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States the plant receives phosphorus (and water) from the fungus.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States what the plant gains from the mycorrhizal association.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the fungus receives sugars, so both partners benefit.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States the fungus receives carbohydrates from the plant, so both benefit.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States what the fungus gains, completing the mutualism.

canonical_answer_1:
Mycorrhizal fungi extend plant root surface area by many times, improving absorption of water and minerals especially phosphorus.

The plant provides sugars (carbohydrates) to the fungus via the phloem; this is a mutualistic symbiosis.

Fungal hyphae explore a much larger soil volume than the plant roots alone and deliver absorbed phosphate and water to the plant; in exchange, the fungus receives carbohydrates from photosynthesis.

stem: A researcher disrupts the expression of a gene encoding a gap junction protein (connexin) in heart muscle cells.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-085

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Gap junctions create direct cytoplasmic connections; ions (the electrical signal) flow through the channels into adjacent cells without crossing membranes.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how gap junctions allow electrical signals to spread between heart muscle cells.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States gap junctions are channels connecting adjacent cells; ions flow directly from one cell to the next, propagating the action potential.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Without functional gap junctions, electrical signals cannot coordinate across cells; contractions become uncoordinated, causing arrhythmia.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Predict what would happen to heart rhythm if connexin proteins were nonfunctional.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States gap junctions fail; electrical signals cannot spread uniformly across the heart; uncoordinated contraction (arrhythmia) results.

canonical_answer_1:
Gap junctions are protein channels connecting adjacent cells, allowing direct cytoplasmic communication of ions and small molecules.

In the heart, gap junctions allow electrical signals (ion flow) to spread rapidly across cardiac muscle cells, coordinating contraction.

Nonfunctional connexins prevent formation of conducting gap-junction channels between adjacent cardiac muscle cells. Depolarization can no longer spread synchronously through the tissue, so contractions become poorly coordinated and the heart develops an arrhythmia.
canonical_answer_2: In the heart, gap junctions allow electrical signals (ion flow) to spread rapidly across cardiac muscle cells, coordinating contraction.

stem: A biologist studying coral reefs notes that as ocean temperatures rise, corals expel their symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) and bleach.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-086

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that zooxanthellae photosynthesize and provide sugars to the coral.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States zooxanthellae perform photosynthesis inside coral tissue, providing sugars.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the algae's photosynthetic contribution to the coral.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the coral supplies CO2 and nutrients to the zooxanthellae.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States the coral provides CO2 and inorganic nutrients to the algae.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States what the coral contributes to the algae in return.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that bleaching/coral death eliminates the reef's physical structure.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States bleached/dead coral loses its structural habitat.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that coral death removes the reef's structural complexity.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that species relying on coral for habitat or food decline, reducing biodiversity.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States many reef species depend on that coral structure for habitat or food, so biodiversity declines.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the consequence for species richness/biodiversity, scoped to habitat/food dependence.

canonical_answer_1:
Zooxanthellae live in coral tissues and provide up to 90% of the coral's energy via photosynthesis.

The coral host releases respiratory CO₂ and inorganic nitrogen or phosphorus compounds that the zooxanthellae can use in photosynthesis and growth.

When thermal stress causes algae expulsion, corals lose their energy source and eventually die if temperatures remain high.

Prolonged bleaching deprives corals of much of their photosynthetic energy and can cause colony death. As the living reef erodes, its complex three-dimensional shelter is lost.

Fish and invertebrates that use branching coral for refuge, feeding, or reproduction lose those resources after reef degradation. Their populations decline or leave, lowering species richness.
canonical_answer_2: When thermal stress causes algae expulsion, corals lose their energy source and eventually die if temperatures remain high.

stem: A scientist studies stabilizing selection in human birth weight, finding that very low and very high birth weights have higher infant mortality.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-087

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that intermediate birth weight maximizes fitness.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States intermediate birth weights have the highest survival/fitness.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the fitness peak at intermediate birth weight.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State the two distinct causes of reduced fitness at each extreme.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States very low and very high birth weights both have lower fitness (underdevelopment vs. delivery complications).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States both tails of the distribution have reduced fitness, with distinct causes.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that stabilizing selection reduces variance without shifting the mean.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States stabilizing selection keeps the population mean unchanged while decreasing phenotypic variance.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States both effects of stabilizing selection: mean unchanged, variance decreases.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that directional selection shifts the mean toward one extreme.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States directional selection shifts the population mean toward one extreme (and may also change variance).
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the contrasting effect of directional selection on the mean.

canonical_answer_1:
Stabilizing selection favors intermediate phenotypes and reduces variation; extreme phenotypes have lower fitness.

Infants at the low-weight extreme have lower survival because organs may be insufficiently developed, whereas very high birth weight increases obstructed-delivery and birth-trauma risk. Selection therefore removes individuals from both tails.

Over time, stabilizing selection reduces variance in the population without shifting the mean. Directional selection, by contrast, favors one phenotypic extreme, shifting the population mean toward that extreme over time rather than preserving it. In short: stabilizing selection preserves the mean and reduces variation, while directional selection shifts the mean.
canonical_answer_2: Over time, stabilizing selection reduces variance in the population without shifting the mean. Directional selection, by contrast, favors one phenotypic extreme, shifting the population mean toward that extreme over time rather than preserving it. In short: stabilizing selection preserves the mean and reduces variation, while directional selection shifts the mean.

title: APBIO-FRQ-S-090

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Defines GPP as total energy fixed by photosynthesis and NPP as GPP minus energy used in autotroph respiration
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Defines GPP as total energy fixed by photosynthesis and NPP as GPP minus energy used in autotroph respiration

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States only NPP energy is stored as biomass and available to consumers
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States only NPP energy is stored as biomass and available to consumers

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State reduced light lowers the rate of photosynthesis, causing both GPP and NPP to fall
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States reduced light lowers the rate of photosynthesis, causing both GPP and NPP to fall
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States reduced light lowers the rate of photosynthesis, causing both GPP and NPP to fall

frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States this reduces the energy available to support consumer populations
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States this reduces the energy available to support consumer populations

canonical_answer_1:
GPP is total photosynthesis; NPP = GPP minus energy lost to autotroph respiration; NPP represents energy available to consumers.

High NPP supports more complex food webs and higher biodiversity.

Less light limits the light reactions and therefore carbon fixation, lowering gross primary productivity. Because respiration still consumes part of production, net primary productivity also falls.

A decrease in NPP means producers add less chemical energy to new biomass. Less energy is then available for herbivores and the higher trophic levels that depend on them.

stem: A scientist introduces a frameshift mutation by inserting one nucleotide into the middle of a protein-coding gene.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-094

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: An insertion alters the reading frame for all downstream codons, changing every amino acid after it; a substitution only affects one codon.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain why a single nucleotide insertion is more disruptive than a single nucleotide substitution.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States an insertion shifts the entire reading frame of all codons downstream; a substitution only changes one codon (one amino acid).

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: A premature stop codon terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein that is missing C-terminal sequences and usually nonfunctional.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explain how a premature stop codon resulting from a frameshift mutation would affect the protein product.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the ribosome terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein that lacks its C-terminal domain and is likely nonfunctional.

canonical_answer_1:
A frameshift mutation shifts the reading frame of all downstream codons, altering every amino acid after the insertion.

Adding one nucleotide changes how every downstream base is partitioned into codons, so many amino acids can change. A one-base substitution leaves the reading frame intact and usually affects only its single codon.

The result is usually a nonfunctional protein; a premature stop codon may also truncate the protein.

When the shifted reading frame generates an early stop codon, the ribosome releases the chain before the normal terminus. The shortened protein lacks downstream C-terminal residues or domains and is likely unstable or nonfunctional.
canonical_answer_2: The result is usually a nonfunctional protein; a premature stop codon may also truncate the protein.

stem: A scientist discovers a bacterium that produces a toxin by means of a mobile genetic element that can jump between chromosomes.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-095

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that a transposon can relocate to a new position in the genome.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States a transposon can move to a new genomic location.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the general fact that transposons relocate within the genome (mechanistic cut-and-paste/copy-and-paste detail not required, per AP Biology CED scope).

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that transposon movement contributes to genetic variation.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains that this relocation is a source of genetic variation in the population.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Connects transposon movement to its role as a genetic-variation source, the CED-scoped framing.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that insertion into a coding region can disrupt the gene sequence.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States transposon insertion can disrupt a gene's coding sequence.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that insertion into coding DNA can break the reading frame or sequence.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that insertion into a regulatory region can alter gene expression.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: States insertion into a regulatory region can alter or inactivate gene expression.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that insertion into a promoter/regulatory region can silence or alter expression.

canonical_answer_1:
Transposons (jumping genes) are DNA sequences that can move to new locations in the genome, sometimes disrupting genes or transferring traits.

Transposons are important in evolution and in the spread of antibiotic resistance genes between bacteria.

If the transposon inserts within an exon, it interrupts the normal coding sequence and may shift the reading frame or introduce stop signals, producing an altered protein.

Insertion into a promoter, enhancer, or other control sequence can block or create regulatory binding sites. Transcription of the nearby toxin gene may therefore decrease, cease, or become inappropriately active.
canonical_answer_2: Transposons are important in evolution and in the spread of antibiotic resistance genes between bacteria.

frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States the guide RNA base-pairs with the target DNA strand, positioning Cas9 to cut at that site

CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 nuclease to a specific DNA sequence, where it makes a double-strand break.

The guide RNA includes an approximately 20-nucleotide targeting region chosen to be complementary to the tumor-suppressor DNA next to a suitable PAM site.

Complementary base pairing anchors the guide RNA at the selected genomic sequence and positions the associated Cas9 nuclease so both DNA strands are cut at that locus.

The cell's error-prone repair (NHEJ) introduces insertions or deletions that disable the gene (knockout).

A functional tumor suppressor monitors damage or checkpoint errors and can pause the cell cycle for repair or direct the cell toward apoptosis instead of division.

stem: Students studying animal behavior observe that male frogs produce species-specific calls, and females approach only males of their own species.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-099

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: The species-specific call is a behavioral prezygotic barrier; females only approach males whose call matches, preventing cross-species mating.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Classify the frog mating call as a type of reproductive isolating mechanism and explain how it prevents hybridization.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States behavioral (prezygotic) isolation; female frogs recognize only conspecific calls and do not approach other species, preventing mating.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Hybrid sterility is postzygotic: mules (horse x donkey) are born healthy but cannot reproduce, reducing hybrid fitness to zero.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Give one example of a postzygotic isolating mechanism and explain how it reduces hybrid fitness.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Must name one: hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility, or hybrid breakdown; explains correctly.

canonical_answer_1:
Behavioral isolation is a prezygotic reproductive barrier where species-specific signals prevent mating between species.

Prezygotic barriers prevent hybrid zygote formation; postzygotic barriers reduce hybrid fitness after fertilization.

Hybrid sterility is a postzygotic barrier: a horse–donkey mule can develop and survive, but mismatched chromosome sets prevent normal meiosis and functional gamete production, so the hybrid leaves no offspring.
canonical_answer_2: Prezygotic barriers prevent hybrid zygote formation; postzygotic barriers reduce hybrid fitness after fertilization.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a)(i) Define synapomorphy and explain why it is more informative for constructing phylogenies than symplesiomorphy (a shared ancestral character).
(a)(ii) Using the character matrix data, construct the most parsimonious cladogram for species A–E, identify the outgroup, and explain your reasoning.
(a)(iii) Explain what "most parsimonious" means in phylogenetic analysis.
(a)(iv) Explain why parsimony is preferred when building cladograms.
title: Phylogenetic Cladogram Construction and Parsimony
stimulus:
Character matrix (1 = character present, 0 = absent):
               | Char 1 | Char 2 | Char 3 | Char 4
Species A      |   0    |   0    |   0    |   0    (outgroup)
Species B      |   1    |   0    |   0    |   0
Species C      |   1    |   1    |   0    |   0
Species D      |   1    |   1    |   1    |   0
Species E      |   1    |   1    |   1    |   1

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that a synapomorphy is a shared character derived from a common ancestor, distinguishing it from an ancestral (underived) character.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Defines synapomorphy as a shared derived character.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: A clear definition distinguishing a derived (newly evolved) character from an ancestral one.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that only shared derived characters indicate recent common ancestry; shared ancestral characters are uninformative because they are shared too broadly.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains why synapomorphies, not symplesiomorphies, are informative for building phylogenies.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Explains that shared ancestral characters (symplesiomorphies) are present broadly across a group and do not distinguish sub-groups, while shared derived characters mark recent common ancestry.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Give the correct topology and identify A as the outgroup because it has none of the derived characters shared by B-E.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Constructs the most-parsimonious cladogram from the matrix, identifies species A as the outgroup, and explains the reasoning.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Correct nested topology (A,(B,(C,(D,E)))); identifies A as the outgroup because it lacks all four derived characters.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that the most parsimonious tree is the one requiring the fewest character-state changes.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains what "most parsimonious" means in phylogenetic analysis.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that the most parsimonious tree requires the fewest evolutionary changes or character-state transitions.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that parsimony is preferred because it requires the fewest unsupported assumptions, such as repeated independent origins or reversals of a character.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains why parsimony is preferred when building cladograms.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: States that parsimony is preferred because it requires the fewest unsupported assumptions, such as independent origins or reversals.

canonical_answer_1:
A synapomorphy is a shared derived character that evolved in the common ancestor of a group and was inherited by its descendants.

It is more useful than a symplesiomorphy because an ancestral character may be shared by many lineages and therefore does not distinguish more recent branches, whereas a shared derived character identifies a more recent common ancestor.

Species A is the outgroup because it lacks all four derived characters. The most parsimonious topology is (A,(B,(C,(D,E)))). Character 1 unites B-E, character 2 unites C-E, character 3 unites D and E, and character 4 is unique to E, so each character needs to arise only once on this tree.

"Most parsimonious" means the tree that requires the fewest total character-state changes.

Parsimony is preferred because it explains the observed character distribution with the fewest unsupported evolutionary assumptions, such as repeated independent origins or reversals of the same character.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question. The molecular clock hypothesis proposes that DNA sequences accumulate mutations at an approximately constant rate over time.

(b)(i) Explain the molecular basis for the molecular clock — why do neutral mutations accumulate at a relatively constant rate?
(b)(ii) Use the data in Table 1 to estimate the divergence time for the third pair (Human–Gorilla) and show your work.
(b)(iii) Describe ONE reason why the molecular clock is not perfectly constant and can give inaccurate divergence estimates.
(b)(iv) Describe a SECOND, distinct reason why the molecular clock is not perfectly constant.
title: Molecular Clock Divergence-Time Calculation
stimulus:
Table 1: Molecular clock data — Cytochrome b sequence divergence
Species pair         | % sequence difference | Known divergence (Mya)
Human–Chimpanzee     |       2.5%            |      5-7 Mya
Rhesus–Baboon        |       5.4%            |     10-12 Mya
Human–Gorilla        |       4.0%            |      ?

Calculation setup: Assume 1% cytochrome b divergence ≈ 2 Mya
(calibrated from the known pairs above)

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: State that neutral mutations are invisible to natural selection, so they accumulate at a roughly constant, selection-independent rate.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains the molecular basis for why neutral mutations accumulate at a relatively constant rate.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Explains that neutral mutations are not acted on by natural selection, so their accumulation rate tracks the underlying mutation rate rather than fluctuating with selective pressure.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Show the calculation 4.0 x 2 = 8.0 Mya using the given calibration.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Calculates the Human-Gorilla divergence time as 8.0 Mya, showing work using the supplied calibration.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Shows 4.0% x 2 Mya/% = 8.0 Mya using the given calibration (1% divergence ≈ 2 Mya).

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Give one valid reason the clock rate can vary, such as generation-time differences or non-neutral sites.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describes one valid reason the molecular clock is not perfectly constant.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Any scientifically valid limitation, e.g. mutation rate varies with generation time, or some sites are under selection rather than neutral.

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Give a second, different valid reason, such as repair-rate differences between lineages or calibration uncertainty.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Describes a second, distinct valid reason the molecular clock is not perfectly constant.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: A second scientifically valid limitation, distinct from the first, e.g. DNA repair-efficiency differences between lineages, or calibration-fossil uncertainty.

canonical_answer_1:
(b)(i) Neutral mutations, by definition, do not affect an organism's fitness and so are not acted on by natural selection; their rate of fixation in a population is governed mainly by the underlying mutation rate, which tends to be relatively stable over time for a given gene and lineage. Because these mutations are not selected for or against, their accumulation approximates a constant, clock-like rate over time, forming the basis of the molecular clock.
(ii) Using the given calibration (1% cytochrome b sequence divergence corresponds to approximately 2 million years): Human-Gorilla divergence of 4.0% times 2 Mya per percent equals approximately 8.0 million years ago.
(iii) Two reasons the molecular clock is not perfectly constant: (1) mutation and generation rates differ among lineages — species with shorter generation times undergo more DNA replications per unit time and tend to accumulate mutations faster than species with longer generation times, so different lineages' clocks tick at different absolute rates; (2) selective pressures vary among genes, lineages, and over time — some genomic regions experience differing degrees of purifying or positive selection in different lineages, causing deviations from a strictly neutral, constant rate of accumulation (differences in DNA repair efficiency and uncertainty/inaccuracy in fossil calibration dates also contribute to clock imperfection).

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(c)(i) Explain how analogous structures (homoplasy) can cause morphological phylogenies to incorrectly group unrelated organisms together.
(c)(ii) Explain why molecular phylogenies are generally considered more reliable than morphological phylogenies for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, and give a specific example of a case where molecular data overturned a morphologically derived phylogeny.
(d)(i)-(d)(iii) A researcher wants to determine whether two geographically isolated populations of mice are separate species or subspecies. Describe THREE lines of evidence the researcher could collect (one per sub-part) and explain how each line of evidence would contribute to a decision.
title: Homoplasy, Molecular Reliability, and Species-Delimitation Evidence

frq_criteria.minimum_fix: Explain that convergently evolved analogous structures can be mistaken for synapomorphies, incorrectly grouping unrelated species.
frq_criteria.learner_facing_text: Explains how homoplasy (analogous structures) can mislead morphological phylogenies.
frq_criteria.evidence_requirements: Analogous structures evolve independently in unrelated lineages under similar selective pressures (convergent evolution); a morphological analysis treating such a structure as a synapomorphy incorrectly groups the unrelated lineages together.

canonical_answer_1:
(c)(i) Homoplasy (analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution) arises when unrelated organisms independently evolve similar traits in response to similar selective pressures or environments, rather than through shared ancestry. If a morphological phylogenetic analysis mistakenly treats these convergent similarities as synapomorphies (shared derived traits indicating common ancestry), it will incorrectly group these unrelated organisms together as if they were closely related, producing an inaccurate tree.
(ii) Molecular phylogenies are generally considered more reliable for resolving deep evolutionary relationships because DNA and protein sequences provide vastly more independent characters (thousands of nucleotide or amino acid positions) than morphology offers (a limited number of visible traits), which reduces the relative influence of any single misleading homoplasious character, and molecular changes are generally less subject to convergent selective pressures than gross external morphology. A well-known example is that molecular data revealed hippopotamuses to be the closest living relatives of whales (Cetacea), a relationship not evident from morphology alone, overturning earlier morphology-based classifications that had grouped whales more closely with other terrestrial mammal groups based on convergent similarities.

(d) Three lines of evidence: (1) Reproductive compatibility/hybridization testing — determining whether the two populations can successfully interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural or controlled conditions; full interbreeding with fertile offspring supports classification as the same species or subspecies, while reduced hybrid viability or sterility supports separate species status. (2) Genetic/DNA sequence divergence — comparing DNA sequence differences (such as mitochondrial DNA or whole-genome divergence) between the two populations; genetic distances comparable to those typically seen between recognized separate species would support species status, while smaller divergence comparable to normal within-species variation would support subspecies status. (3) Morphological and ecological differentiation — comparing consistent, diagnostic differences in physical traits (body size, coloration, skull shape) and ecological niche (habitat use, diet, behavior) between the populations; substantial and consistent diagnostic differences support species-level distinction, whereas overlapping or continuously varying traits support classification as subspecies.

stem: Which chain of reasoning correctly connects the cellular membrane change to the whole-organism survival outcome in dehydrated wild-type mice?
title: APBIO-MCQ-025
stimulus: Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) is a water channel protein in kidney collecting duct cells regulated by antidiuretic hormone (ADH). In dehydrated animals, ADH is secreted from the posterior pituitary and causes AQP2-containing vesicles inside collecting duct cells to fuse with the apical (urine-facing) plasma membrane, inserting AQP2 channels within 15 minutes. AQP2 density on the apical membrane increases 5-fold. In mice with AQP2 mutations preventing hormone-regulated membrane insertion, urine output is 10× greater than in wild-type mice; these mice die within 48 hours without unlimited water access.

mcq_choices.rationale: The kidney medulla is hyperosmotic relative to tubular urine. AQP2 insertion into the apical membrane lets water move down its osmotic gradient from the tubule into the medulla and ultimately into blood. Without AQP2 insertion, water stays in the tubule and is excreted as dilute urine, as seen in the mutant mice.
mcq_choices.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 inserts into the apical membrane → increased water permeability of the collecting duct → water moves osmotically from the tubule into the hyperosmotic kidney medulla → urine becomes concentrated → body water is conserved

mcq_choices.rationale: This inverts the mechanism. ADH causes AQP2 insertion, not degradation. Fewer channels would produce the mutant phenotype (excess dilute urine), not water conservation. The chain of causation is reversed.
mcq_choices.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 is degraded from the apical membrane → fewer water channels → less water reabsorption → more dilute urine → blood becomes hyperosmotic → kidney retains water by osmosis

mcq_choices.rationale: AQP2 inserts into the apical (urine-facing) membrane, not the basolateral membrane. Water must first cross the apical membrane from the tubular lumen into the cell before exiting via constitutively expressed aquaporins on the basolateral side. Moving water from blood into the tubule would worsen dehydration, not correct it.
mcq_choices.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 inserts into the basolateral (blood-facing) membrane → water moves from blood into the kidney tubule → urine becomes dilute → blood volume increases → dehydration is reversed

mcq_choices.rationale: AQP2 is a water channel; it does not block sodium channels. Na⁺ transport in the collecting duct is a separate regulatory pathway not tested by this item.
mcq_choices.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 blocks sodium channels on the apical membrane → Na⁺ accumulates in the tubule → high tubular osmolarity retains water in the lumen → concentrated urine is produced

stem: Which best explains why apoptosis — rather than necrosis — is essential for sculpting the spaces between developing digits?
title: APBIO-MCQ-030
stimulus: During human hand development, interdigital cells undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis). Caspase enzymes are activated by cytochrome c release from mitochondria (intrinsic pathway) and by death-ligand binding to surface receptors (extrinsic pathway). Active caspases systematically dismantle the cell: cleaving cytoskeletal proteins, fragmenting DNA, and producing membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed by neighboring cells without rupturing. In necrosis, cellular contents spill into surrounding tissue, triggering inflammation. Mice lacking the pro-apoptotic genes Bax and Bak retain webbing between their digits.

mcq_choices.rationale: Necrosis may avoid the energy cost of caspase activation, but efficiency is not why apoptosis is required here: necrosis triggers inflammation that would damage the neighboring digit tissue, which is the actual reason the controlled, non-inflammatory apoptotic pathway is needed for precise sculpting.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Necrosis would clear the interdigital cells more efficiently than apoptosis because it does not require ATP-dependent caspase activation

mcq_choices.rationale: Apoptotic cells package themselves into membrane-bound bodies that are cleanly phagocytosed, releasing no inflammatory signals. This allows selective elimination of specific cells — the interdigital mesenchyme — without damaging the neighboring digit progenitor cells. Necrosis would trigger inflammation that could disrupt digit development. The Bax/Bak knockout phenotype directly confirms that pro-apoptotic signaling is required for interdigital clearance.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Apoptosis eliminates interdigital cells in an orderly, contained manner that prevents inflammation and preserves the integrity of adjacent digit tissue, allowing precise sculpting of the hand

mcq_choices.rationale: Necrosis is typically faster than apoptosis (minutes vs. hours). The developmental advantage of apoptosis is its controlled, inflammation-free nature — not its speed.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Apoptosis is faster than necrosis, ensuring interdigital cells are eliminated within the narrow developmental window before digit formation is complete

mcq_choices.rationale: This reverses the knockout result. Bax and Bak are intrinsic-pathway genes; losing them blocks apoptosis and causes webbing, showing the intrinsic pathway is required for interdigital clearance -- not that the extrinsic pathway alone is sufficient without it.
mcq_choices.choice_text: The Bax/Bak knockout result shows that the extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway alone is sufficient to trigger interdigital apoptosis, since Bax and Bak are intrinsic-pathway genes

stem: If the IP₃ receptor on the ER is blocked pharmacologically, what effect on PKC activity is most directly predicted?
title: APBIO-MCQ-033
stimulus: Activation of a cell-surface receptor triggers cleavage of a plasma-membrane phospholipid into two second messengers: IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ diffuses to the ER membrane and opens ligand-gated Ca²⁺ channels, releasing stored Ca²⁺ into the cytoplasm. DAG remains anchored in the plasma membrane. Protein kinase C (PKC) is activated by the simultaneous presence of both DAG at the membrane and elevated cytoplasmic Ca²⁺. When both co-activators are present, PKC activity is maximal; DAG or Ca²⁺ alone provides only weak partial activation.

mcq_choices.rationale: IP₃ activates Ca²⁺ release from the ER; it does not directly activate PKC. PKC is activated by DAG (still present) and Ca²⁺ (now absent). Confusing the IP₃ function (Ca²⁺ release) with direct PKC activation is a common error.
mcq_choices.choice_text: PKC activity is completely eliminated because IP₃ is the direct activator of PKC

mcq_choices.rationale: Blocking the IP₃ receptor removes Ca²⁺ as a co-activator but does not affect DAG generation or membrane localization. Per the stimulus, DAG alone provides only weak partial activation, so PKC activity drops substantially without reaching zero.
mcq_choices.choice_text: PKC activity is substantially reduced, though not eliminated, because losing IP₃-receptor-gated Ca²⁺ release removes one of PKC's two required co-activators, while DAG generation is unaffected

mcq_choices.rationale: The stimulus explicitly states that DAG alone provides only weak partial activation and that maximal PKC activity requires both DAG and Ca²⁺. This choice contradicts the given information.
mcq_choices.choice_text: PKC activity is completely unaffected because DAG alone is sufficient for full PKC activation without Ca²⁺

mcq_choices.rationale: The stimulus describes cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ elevation as coming specifically from IP₃-receptor-gated ER release; blocking that receptor removes the described source. Nothing in the stimulus establishes an alternative plasma-membrane Ca²⁺-entry pathway in this system, so this choice introduces a claim the stimulus does not support.
mcq_choices.choice_text: PKC activity is unchanged because Ca²⁺ enters from outside the cell instead

stem: Which best explains why this patient's thyroid hormone levels remain elevated despite already-high circulating T3?
title: APBIO-MCQ-046
stimulus: Thyroid hormone (T3) homeostasis depends on a negative feedback loop: low T3 → hypothalamus releases TRH → pituitary releases TSH → thyroid gland produces T3 → elevated T3 feeds back to suppress both TRH and TSH release. A patient is found to have a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (benign tumor) that secretes TSH autonomously. The patient's serum T3 is 4× the normal upper limit.

mcq_choices.rationale: In normal physiology, elevated T3 suppresses TSH release, closing the feedback loop. The adenoma bypasses this by producing TSH regardless of T3 concentration, so the thyroid keeps receiving stimulatory signals and maintains excess T3 production -- a feedback loop disrupted by autonomous hormone secretion.
mcq_choices.choice_text: The pituitary adenoma secretes TSH independently of T3 feedback, so continuous TSH stimulation keeps driving the thyroid to overproduce T3 despite already-elevated levels

mcq_choices.rationale: Reduced thyroid sensitivity to TSH is a real endocrine mechanism, but it would explain elevated TSH driving T3 back to normal -- not a tumor that secretes TSH autonomously and drives T3 to 4x the normal upper limit. It does not fit this stimulus's specific finding.
mcq_choices.choice_text: The thyroid has become less sensitive to TSH, so more TSH is required to maintain a normal T3 level

mcq_choices.rationale: A TSH-secreting adenoma producing 4× normal T3 is not an incidental finding — it is causal. The thyroid is responding to excessive TSH stimulation; the primary defect is in the pituitary, not the thyroid. The thyroid remains TSH-dependent.
mcq_choices.choice_text: The thyroid gland has become autonomous and produces T3 independently of TSH; the pituitary adenoma is an incidental finding unrelated to elevated T3

mcq_choices.rationale: T3 normally suppresses TSH release at the pituitary — this is negative feedback, not positive. A T3-driven increase in TSH secretion would be an inversion of the known feedback relationship. The adenoma secretes TSH constitutively (not in response to T3), and T3 does not stimulate TSH in normal physiology.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Elevated T3 activates a positive feedback loop at the pituitary, causing the adenoma to secrete even more TSH in response to high hormone levels

stem: Under which condition does Hamilton's rule predict that an altruistic behavior will be favored by natural selection?
title: APBIO-MCQ-088
stimulus: Altruistic behaviors reduce the fitness of the actor while increasing the fitness of the recipient — a puzzle for classical Darwinian selection, which favors traits that increase individual fitness. William Hamilton proposed that altruism can be explained by inclusive fitness: an individual's fitness includes not just its own reproductive success but also the effect of its actions on copies of its genes present in relatives. Hamilton's rule states that altruism is favored when: rB > C, where r = coefficient of relatedness (probability that a gene in the actor is identical by descent to a gene in the recipient), B = fitness benefit to the recipient, and C = fitness cost to the actor.

mcq_choices.rationale: This inverts Hamilton's rule. rB > C is the condition for altruism to be favored — the relatedness-weighted benefit must EXCEED the cost. If C > rB, the cost outweighs the inclusive fitness benefit and the altruistic allele would be disfavored by selection.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Altruism is favored when C > rB — the cost to the actor must exceed the relatedness-weighted benefit to the recipient

mcq_choices.rationale: Hamilton's rule rB > C unpacked: r (coefficient of relatedness) weights the benefit by how likely the recipient shares the altruistic allele -- full sibling r=0.5, offspring r=0.5, first cousin r=0.125. Even at personal cost, an actor can propagate copies of its alleles through relatives. Classic example: a worker honeybee (r=0.75 to sisters in a haplodiploid colony) sacrifices direct reproduction but raises sisters who share 3/4 of its genes -- rB may exceed C. This is kin selection. A remark often attributed to J.B.S. Haldane (exact wording varies by source) captures the logic: he would risk his life for two brothers or eight cousins -- both give rB = 1, at the breakeven threshold with C = 1 for one life.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Altruism is favored when rB > C: the benefit to the recipient (B), discounted by the probability of shared ancestry (r), must exceed the cost to the actor (C); even if the actor loses direct fitness, the same allele is more likely to be present -- and thus propagated -- in the relative, so the altruistic allele can increase in frequency if it causes enough copies of itself to survive in relatives

mcq_choices.rationale: The cost is never irrelevant — Hamilton's rule is a quantitative threshold. Even among full siblings (r=0.5), altruism is only favored if 0.5 × B > C, i.e., if B > 2C. A very costly act with small benefit (e.g., C=10, B=1) would not be favored even between full siblings: 0.5×1 = 0.5 < 10. The magnitudes of B and C always matter.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Altruism is always favored among close relatives regardless of the cost-to-benefit ratio, because shared genes make the cost irrelevant

mcq_choices.rationale: Hamilton's rule applies universally across sexually reproducing species with any relatedness structure. Altruism is documented in diploid organisms: ground squirrel alarm calls (r=0.25–0.5 among relatives), cooperative breeding in birds (helpers at the nest). Haplodiploidy elevates r among sisters in hymenoptera, facilitating eusociality, but it is not required for altruism to evolve.
mcq_choices.choice_text: Altruism only evolves in eusocial insects because their unusual haplodiploid genetics makes r > 0.5 between sisters; altruism cannot evolve in diploid species
